title: Galaxy Airlines 203
summary: The Lockheed Electra experienced vibrations shortly after takeoff due to ground crew error in loading. The pilots mistakenly attributed the vibrations to a faulty engine and reduced power to all four engines simultaneously, which lowered lift forces and caused the aircraft to stall. The aircraft crashed nose-high onto Reno Field approximately 1.5 miles short of the runway end.
probable_cause: Pilot error in misidentifying the source of vibrations during takeoff and reducing power to all engines instead of feathering a suspected failed engine, combined with ground crew cargo loading error that caused the initial vibrations.

factors.evidence: Ground crew error when loading cargo to the aft compartment
Aircraft stall caused by loss of lift when pilots reduced power to all four engines
Aircraft began descending in a nose-high attitude, continued losing altitude despite pilots adding power back
Pilots mistakenly thought vibrations were caused by faulty engine rather than ground crew error
Pilots rushed through required checklists and abandoned pre-departure briefing due to late arrival

events.text: Ground crew finished loading approximately 67 pieces of luggage into the aft compartment, causing an uneven weight distribution
Aircraft took off from Reno-Tahoe and immediately experienced significant vibrations
Pilots reduced power to all four engines, thinking the vibrations indicated a faulty engine
Airspeed decreased as the aircraft lost thrust from all engines, causing the aircraft to stall in a nose-high attitude
Pilots tried to climb and added power back to engines, but aircraft continued losing altitude
Aircraft crashed onto Reno Field at 105 knots in a nose-high condition, just 1.5 miles short of the runway end

title: Iberia Airlines 610

agencies.name: Civil Aviation Accident and Incident Investigation Commission

summary: Iberia Flight 610, a Boeing 727 on a short domestic hop from Madrid to Bilbao, crashed into a ravine on Mount Oiz on 19 February 1985 after its left wing struck a television antenna during the approach in fog, killing all 141 passengers and 7 crew. Spanish investigators found the autopilot's altitude-select system had failed to engage, letting the aircraft descend past its target altitude, and that the crew misread the altitude alerts and kept descending during a turn that took them into the fog-shrouded mountain.
probable_cause: Spanish investigators attributed the crash to pilot error: the autopilot's altitude select system failed to engage for undetermined reasons, and the crew misinterpreted the altitude alarms, continuing a descent below safe altitude during a turn that flew the aircraft into Mount Oiz in fog.

factors.evidence: The autopilot's altitude select system failed to engage due to undetermined reasons, enabling the aircraft to descend past its target altitude.
The altitude alert went off and the crew continued the descent as the second tonal alarm, which would have confirmed level-off, had not sounded.
The weather conditions at the time were cloudy with fog, with 4 km of visibility, as the aircraft flew 177 ft above Mount Oiz.
The crew began to initiate the loop back towards the airport by making a tight turn to the left, during which they would bypass Mount Oiz.
The aircraft's left wing collided with an antenna of the Euskal Telebistarues television tower at 3,356 ft, shearing the wing off and causing the aircraft to crash into a ravine.

events.text: During the approach the autopilot's altitude select system failed to engage for undetermined reasons, letting the aircraft descend past its target altitude.
The altitude alert sounded but the crew continued the descent because the second tonal alarm, which would have confirmed reaching the intended altitude, had not sounded.
The crew began a tight turn to the left to loop back toward the airport, a maneuver intended to bypass Mount Oiz, while flying in fog with 4 km of visibility.
Flying 177 ft above Mount Oiz in landing configuration at 239 mph, the aircraft's left wing collided with an antenna of the Euskal Telebistarues television tower at 3,356 ft.
Losing all lift from the left side, the aircraft rolled left, hit dozens of pine trees, and dived into a ravine in inverted condition, killing all 141 passengers and 7 crew.

title: Air India 182
summary: Air India Flight 182, a Boeing 747 flying from Toronto toward Mumbai via Montreal and London, exploded over the Atlantic near Ireland on 23 June 1985, killing all 329 aboard. Investigators found the recorders stopped at the same instant and blast damage in the forward cargo bay, concluding a bomb planted by Sikh terrorists from the Babbar Khalsa brought the aircraft down; the bomb had been checked as unaccompanied baggage onto a connecting flight from Vancouver.
probable_cause: Investigators concluded a bomb, planted by Sikh separatists from the Babbar Khalsa and hidden in a Sanyo stereo tuner checked as unaccompanied baggage from Vancouver, detonated near the forward cargo hold and brought the aircraft down.

factors.evidence: the Boeing 747... exploded near the coast of Ireland from a bomb planted by Sikh terrorists from the Babbar Khalsa
in both cases the planes were carrying bags without the passenger who checked them in
damage to parts recovered from the forward cargo bay consistent with a blast
it was probably a bomb near the forward cargo hold that brought the plane down suddenly

events.text: Two bombs were checked onto Canadian Pacific Air Lines flights from Vancouver, one to connect with Flight 301 at Tokyo and one with Flight 182 at Montreal.
The bomb intended for Flight 301 detonated early at Tokyo's Narita Airport, killing two baggage handlers as the suitcase was being transferred to the Air India 747.
The 747 serving the Montreal-London segment of Flight 182 exploded near the coast of Ireland on the morning of 23 June 1985, killing all 329 aboard.
The cockpit voice and flight data recorders stopped recording at the same instant, and damage to parts from the forward cargo bay was consistent with a blast.

notes: no formal air-safety board named in text; RCMP led the criminal investigation described
structural_failure/explosive_decompression inferred from 'blast damage' and 'brought the plane down suddenly'; no bomb debris was recovered from the ocean

title: Aeroflot 7425
summary: The Tu-154 climbed to 11600 m where it encountered non-standard high temperatures 16.5 degrees C above normal. The crew changed the autopilot to gain speed, causing pitch-down. When the aircraft neared stall warning threshold, the alarm blown a fuse and stopped. The crew misidentified engine compressor stall, making incorrect throttle inputs. The aircraft entered a flat spin and crashed in the Kyzylkum Desert.
probable_cause: Crew made incorrect throttle responses to an engine compressor stall at high altitude with high temperature conditions and high aircraft weight, resulting in loss of thrust and uncontrolled flat spin entry.

factors.evidence: Non-standard outside air temperature 16.5 degrees C higher than standard at cruise altitude disrupted engine airflow
Engine compressor stall caused aircraft shaking and disruption to engine thrust
Flight engineer thought the shaking was a compressor stall and ordered the crew to decrease speed
Crew both decreased and increased speed instead of following proper procedure, captain continued to hold altitude
Aircraft entered flat spin at cruising altitude, lost speed from 400 kph to 290 kph, remained in spin for 2 minutes 33 seconds

events.text: Aircraft took off from Karshi 4 hours late, climbed to 11600 m in non-standard temperature 16.5 degrees C above normal
Crew changed autopilot to gain speed, aircraft pitched down
Crew pulled aircraft up, approached critical angle of attack, stall alarm stopped due to blown fuse
Aircraft entered critical angle of attack, airflow to engines disrupted causing shaking and compressor stall
Flight engineer ordered crew to decrease speed thinking it was compressor stall, crew both decreased and increased speed
Aircraft remained in flat spin for 2 minutes 33 seconds, speed decreased to 290 kph, crashed in Uchkuduk District in Kyzylkum Desert

title: Delta Air Lines 191
summary: Delta Air Lines Flight 191, an L-1011 TriStar, encountered a microburst while on approach to Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport on 2 August 1985. The aircraft impacted terrain over 1 mile short of the runway. The NTSB determined the crash resulted from the crew's decision to fly through a thunderstorm, the lack of procedures or training to avoid or escape microbursts, and the lack of hazard information on wind shear. The descent rate exceeded 3000 feet per minute with angle of attack over 30 degrees.
probable_cause: The National Transportation Safety Board determined that the crash resulted from the flight crew's decision to fly through a thunderstorm, the lack of procedures or training to avoid or escape microbursts and the lack of hazard information on wind shear.

factors.evidence: the Lockheed L-1011 TriStar encountered a microburst while on approach to land at DFW
the flight crew flew through a thunderstorm
the lack of procedures or training to avoid or escape microbursts
At 18:05:44, with the aircraft descending at more than 3000 ft/min the ground proximity warning system sounded
the aircraft began a descent from which it never recovered with angle of attack over 30 degrees
the aircraft impacted ground just over 1 mile short of the runway
the aircraft struck water tanks and disintegrated

events.text: The approach controller asked Flight 191 to reduce its speed to 150 knots and handed the flight over to the tower controller.
Price commented, Lightning coming out of that one. Right ahead of us.
At 18:05:36, Connors exclaimed, Hang on to the son of a bitch and the aircraft began a descent from which it never recovered.
At 18:05:44, with the aircraft descending at more than 3000 ft/min the ground proximity warning system sounded.
The captain responded by declaring TOGA, aviation shorthand for the order to apply maximum thrust and abort a landing by going around.
At 18:05:52, the aircraft's landing gear made contact with a plowed field 6336 ft north of the runway and 360 ft east of the runway centerline.

title: Japan Air Lines 123
summary: Japan Air Lines Flight 123 suffered explosive decompression 12 minutes after takeoff from Tokyo when an aft pressure bulkhead, repaired seven years earlier, finally failed, rupturing all four hydraulic systems and ejecting the vertical stabiliser. The crew flew under minimal control for 32 minutes before the Boeing 747 crashed near Mount Takamagahara, killing 520 of 524 aboard. The 1978 repair had used two splice plates instead of Boeing's specified continuous plate, cutting fatigue resistance to about 70 percent of a correct repair.
probable_cause: The aft pressure bulkhead, repaired after a 1978 tailstrike with two splice plates instead of Boeing's specified continuous plate, gradually cracked under pressurization cycles and failed after 12,318 flights, causing decompression that severed all hydraulic lines and left the aircraft uncontrollable.

factors.evidence: Boeing repair technicians had used two splice plates parallel to the stress crack, negating the effectiveness of a row of rivets
the post-repair inspection by JAL did not discover the defect, as it was covered by overlapping plates
the bulkhead gradually began cracking near the row of rivets... when it finally failed
rapid decompression ruptured the lines of all four hydraulic systems
with many of its flight controls disabled, the aircraft became uncontrollable

events.text: During the 1978 tailstrike on landing at Osaka's Itami Airport, the pilot excessively flared the aircraft on a second touchdown, cracking open the aft pressure bulkhead.
Boeing technicians repaired the bulkhead with two splice plates instead of one continuous splice plate with three rows of rivets as required, and JAL's post-repair inspection missed the defect.
Twelve minutes after takeoff the faultily repaired bulkhead failed, causing decompression that ruptured all four hydraulic systems and ejected the vertical stabiliser.
With flight controls disabled the aircraft became uncontrollable, and the crew flew under minimal control for 32 minutes before the final crash.
In a 40-degree bank the right wing clipped a ridge near Mount Takamagahara, and the aircraft flipped over and struck another ridge before exploding.

title: British Airtours 28M
summary: Flight 28M aborted takeoff after a loud thump at 07:13 BST. A combustor can in the left engine had ruptured and its dome struck the wing fuel tank, allowing fuel to pour onto hot engine gases. A fire developed rapidly inside the fuselage. Although the aircraft stopped safely, the fire spread catastrophically due to flammable cabin interior materials, toxic fumes, and aircraft layout. Most fatalities resulted from smoke inhalation rather than burns.
probable_cause: A maintenance error in the repair or overhaul of the number 9 combustor can led to rupture. The can's dome was ejected and penetrated an underwing fuel tank access panel. Design vulnerabilities in the tank panel location and aircraft hull, combined with flammable cabin materials, allowed the fire to become uncontrollable.

factors.evidence: The No. 9 combustor can on the port engine ruptured
A section of the combustor can was ejected forcibly into an underwing fuel tank access panel
The vulnerability of the wing tank access panels to impact and the vulnerability of the aircraft hull to external fire
The extremely toxic nature of the emissions from the burning interior materials
Of those unable to escape, 48 died as a result of incapacitation and subsequently lethal toxic gas and smoke inhalation

events.text: Loud thump heard during takeoff roll on runway 24
Fire warnings sounded in flight deck nine seconds after the thump was heard
Tower controller suggested evacuating passengers to the right side
Aircraft came to complete stop on runway; fire had developed in left engine
Of those unable to escape, 48 died as a result of incapacitation and subsequently lethal toxic gas and smoke inhalation

title: Arrow Air 1285R
summary: Arrow Air Flight 1285R stalled and crashed shortly after takeoff from Gander, Newfoundland on December 12, 1985. The aircraft had accumulated ice contamination on the wings' leading edges during its earlier approach and refueling stop at Gander. The aircraft was not de-iced prior to takeoff, and the ice buildup degraded lift, resulting in a stall at low altitude from which recovery was not possible.
probable_cause: The most probable cause of the stall was ice contamination on the leading edge and upper surface of the wing following freezing precipitation exposure without de-icing before takeoff, combined with high drag and reduced lift conditions and possibly underestimated onboard weight.

factors.evidence: The aircraft stalled at low altitude from which recovery was not possible.
Ice contamination on the leading edge and upper surface of the wing resulted from precipitation conditions favorable for ice formation and freezing and frozen precipitation.
Prior to takeoff the aircraft had not been de-iced despite exposure to freezing and frozen precipitation.
Underestimated onboard weight may have compounded the effects of the contamination.
A non-functioning cockpit area microphone went undetected for an indeterminate number of flights, and no steps on standard checklists tested its functionality.
The defect in the cockpit area microphone went undetected due to no testing procedure on standard checklists.

events.text: During approach to Gander, precipitation conditions were favorable for formation of ice on wings.
After landing, aircraft remained exposed to freezing and frozen precipitation without de-icing.
Aircraft began takeoff roll on runway 22, rotated at 167 knots after 51 seconds, showing difficulty gaining altitude.
Airspeed reached 172 knots then decreased; aircraft descended after crossing Trans-Canada Highway 900 feet from runway departure end.
Aircraft struck terrain just short of Gander Lake approximately 3500 feet beyond runway departure end, broke up and exploded.
